thought: I've had a hard day. I deserve this.
body: You probably did have a hard day, and you probably do deserve something. That part is true and it isn't worth arguing with. The only question is whether this particular thing delivers what you're actually asking it for. It relieves about twenty minutes. The hard day is still there at the end of it.
move: Don't argue with the thought. Let it stand, exactly as it is, and set a timer for ten minutes. If it's still there after, you'll have decided with your eyes open instead of on the way past the cupboard.
line: The ache is real. It's the object that's wrong. — Augustine, on disordered desire

body: This is the expensive one. The research on it is unusually clear: the first slip costs very little. What costs is the verdict that comes after it, because that's what turns one thing into an evening. Polivy and Herman called it the what-the-hell effect, and it's driven by shame, not by hunger.
move: Skip the verdict. Not the accountability, just the courtroom. The next choice is a fresh one and it starts now, not tomorrow morning.
line: The son had a whole speech prepared. He never got to finish it. — Luke 15:21-22

thought: It's after four and I'm starving.
body: Genuine hunger and the pull of habit feel almost identical from the inside, and they arrive at the same hour because that's the hour you trained. Hunger comes in waves rather than a rising line. If you leave it alone, it usually crests and drops within about twenty minutes, whether or not you do anything about it.
move: Water, then something with your hands for twenty minutes. Don't white-knuckle it — just watch the wave without steering into it.
line: To wait for the lawful moment for breaking the fast. — Cassian, Institutes 5.23

body: Monday is doing a specific job here, which is to let tonight off the hook. It feels like a plan. It's really a permission slip with a date on it. And the version of you that arrives on Monday inherits whatever tonight decides.
move: Don't wait for a clean edge. There isn't one. The next choice available to you is the only one that was ever on offer.
line: Nothing harsh, nothing burdensome. — Rule of St. Benedict, Prologue

body: Sometimes that's completely true. The thought isn't lying to you every time it shows up, which is exactly what makes it effective. The useful question isn't whether it's true — it's whether you're asking it while calm or while already standing in the kitchen.
move: If you decided this earlier today, go with it. If you're deciding it right now, at the fridge, that's the tell. Wait ten minutes and ask again.
line: Decide in consolation what you'll do in desolation. — after Ignatius

thought: Why do I keep doing this?
body: Because it works. That's the honest answer and it's not a flattering one, but it's not a damning one either. Eating for comfort is a solution that reliably delivers relief in under a minute. Nothing else on the shelf is that fast. You didn't pick it because you're weak; you picked it because it works, briefly.
move: Name what you actually wanted — rest, quiet, comfort, an end to the day. Then ask whether any part of that is available right now by another route.
line: Man does not live by bread alone. — Matthew 4:4

body: Set that word down for a second. It has never been a muscle, and treating it as one mostly produces people who conclude they were issued a small one. What's actually happening is a system built to make this hard: the food is engineered, it's four steps away, and you're tired.
move: Change one thing about the room rather than one thing about yourself. Move it, close it, leave the house. Environment beats intention and always has.
line: Grace meets nature where nature actually is.

thought: Nobody would even notice if I quit.
body: Probably true. This was never being done for an audience, which is its own kind of freedom — nobody is watching, so nobody is scoring. The flip side is that the only person who can decide it still matters is the one reading this.
move: Do the smallest version. Three taps. That's the whole ask tonight.
line: Fasting should, as far as possible, be hidden and concealed. — Cassian, Institutes 5.23.3

body: A week isn't an object that can break. It's seven separate days, and five or six of them are unaffected by whatever happened in one. The all-or-nothing read is the single most reliable predictor of stopping altogether, which is the only outcome here that would actually cost you something.
move: Never miss twice. That's the whole rule and it's the only one that survives real life.
line: His mercies are new every morning. — Lamentations 3:22-23

thought: I'm doing everything right and nothing's happening.
body: That's genuinely demoralising and it's also genuinely common. Weight moves in steps and plateaus, not on a slope, and the interval between doing the work and seeing the work is long enough to break most people's faith in the connection. The behaviour is still doing what it does.
move: Look at the last two weeks of check-ins, not the number. That's the thing you actually control and it's the thing that predicts the outcome.
line: You will reap at harvest time if you do not give up. — Galatians 6:9

thought: I just want to feel something else.
body: That's the clearest and most honest version of the thought, and it deserves to be taken seriously rather than corrected. Food changes the channel fast. It's a real tool and it works. The trouble is only that it works for about as long as it takes to eat.
move: You don't have to fix the feeling to get through the next ten minutes. Let it be there and do something small and physical — outside, cold water, a shower.
line: He did not deny the cup. He asked, and then he stayed. — Gethsemane

thought: This is stupid and I want to delete the app.
body: Fair enough. Sometimes it is stupid, and the impulse to bin it usually shows up right after a day you didn't like, which means it's the day talking, not the judgement. Delete it in a week if you still want to. The thought doesn't need to be argued with — just not obeyed tonight.
move: Close it and come back whenever. Nothing here resets and nothing is keeping score against you.
line: You can always come back. That is the entire mechanism. — CCC 1439
